question:
For a real parameter $k$, consider the function $f(x)=x^3-3x^2+kx+2$.

(a) Determine all values of $k$ for which $f'(x)\geq 0$ for every real $x$, and hence $f$ is increasing on $\mathbb{R}$.

(b) For the least value of $k$ obtained in part (a), find the critical point of $f$.

(c) For values of $k$ greater than this least value, determine whether the function has any critical point.
explanation:
(a)
Differentiation
$$f'(x)=3x^2-6x+k$$
Completing the square,
$$f'(x)=3(x-1)^2+k-3$$
Since $3(x-1)^2\geq 0$ for every real $x$, the least value of $f'(x)$ is $k-3$, attained at $x=1$.
For $f'(x)\geq 0$ for every real $x$, we require
$$k-3\geq 0$$
Therefore,
$$k\geq 3$$
Hence, $f$ is increasing on $\mathbb{R}$ for $k\geq 3$.

(b)
The least permissible value is $k=3$. In this case,
$$f'(x)=3(x-1)^2$$
Thus,
$$f'(x)=0\iff x=1$$
Therefore, the critical point is $x=1$.

(c)
For $k>3$,
$$f'(x)=3(x-1)^2+k-3>0$$
for every real $x$. Therefore, $f'(x)$ never vanishes and the function is differentiable everywhere.
Hence, for $k>3$, the function has no critical point and is strictly increasing throughout $\mathbb{R}$.

options.A:
(a) $k>3$
(b) At $k=3$, critical point $x=0$
(c) For $k>3$, two critical points occur
options.B:
(a) $k\leq3$
(b) At $k=3$, critical point $x=1$
(c) For $k>3$, there is one critical point
options.C:
(a) $k\geq3$
(b) At $k=3$, critical point $x=1$
(c) For $k>3$, there is no critical point
options.D:
(a) $k\geq0$
(b) At $k=0$, critical point $x=1$
(c) For $k>0$, there is no critical point
